bibliography.abstract: As LLMs have become a flashpoint for scientific research, computer scientists and STS scholars have advocated the use of open-weight models. Since LLM research has matured and more high-quality model families are available, have researchers adopted open-weight models? We present the first systematic study of model selection in scientific research, analyzing 21 million full-text articles through June 2026 from the Semantic Scholar Open Research Corpus (S2ORC). We employ a mixed NLP pipeline to extract model occurrences in article full text and determine whether they are used or merely mentioned by researchers. We divide our corpus into single- and multi-model family studies, which we take as a proxy for applied and foundational AI research. We find GPT-family models dominate both single- and multi-family research, but that both areas are becoming more diverse over time. In single-family papers, open-weight model use rises steadily, reaching 44.0% in 2026. However, we find that recent growth is driven by the availability of high-quality open-weight Chinese models. Further, a logistic regression model finds that open-weight adoption is heterogeneously distributed, estimating that researchers at Chinese institutions have 2.23 times the odds of using an open-weight model, accounting for 44.0% of the increase in open-weight adoption since 2023. A complementary multinomial model shows this association is concentrated in Chinese open-weight models: in 2026, their adjusted use is 37.1% among papers with Chinese affiliations, a 27.9 percentage-point over papers with no observed China link. These findings suggest that open-weight adoption in science is not a general turn toward open science, but part of a broader realignment of model ecosystems in which platforms and markets, and the sociocultural and geopolitical contexts which shape them, determine which AI systems become scientific instruments.
bibliography.title: Who Uses Open-Weight Models? China and the Shifting Geography of AI in Science

en.caveats: The study relies on model mentions within scientific publications as a proxy for actual research adoption and uses single- versus multi-model family studies to categorize applied versus foundational AI research.
en.what: This study analyzes 21 million full-text scientific articles through June 2026 from the Semantic Scholar Open Research Corpus to track the adoption of open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs). Using a mixed NLP pipeline to distinguish model use from mere mentions, the analysis reveals that while GPT-family models dominate, open-weight model use in single-family papers rose to 44.0% in 2026. Logistic and multinomial regression models show this growth is heavily driven by Chinese institutions, whose researchers have 2.23 times the odds of using open-weight models, with their adjusted use of Chinese open-weight models reaching 37.1% in 2026.
en.why: It demonstrates that the adoption of open-weight models in scientific research is not a uniform shift toward open science, but is instead highly stratified by geopolitical context and the regional availability of specific model ecosystems.
